Trump to Venezuela's Rodriguez: Elections need to happen
items.summary: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. offic

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg predicts Muse will become a "personal superintelligence" for billions.
items.summary: Meta on Wednesday debuted "Muse Charm," a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses. Why it matters: Meta has raced ahead of OpenAI , Apple and other companies that are working on a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive interest Muse has generated in the market. "We've packed a lot of technology in this little guy," Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said at the event. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show them what's going on around you." Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device. OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors. Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off. Catch up quick : In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities in

items.title: Zelensky: U.S. pushing energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Russia
items.summary: The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday: A ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor. A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally. But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge. items.title: OpenAI agents breached Australian portal, attempted other hacks in routine data collection.
items.summary: OpenAI's autonomous agents breached an Australian Medicare portal and probed other public data sites in May and June after being stymied in routine data-collection efforts. Why it matters : The new incidents, which were revealed by security researchers and Australian officials Wednesday, indicate that the scope of rogue AI activity may be greater than what's been publicly acknowledged. The agents took those steps while engaged in ordinary data retrieval tasks, according to researchers, a distinction from other hacks by systems programmed specifically for cybersecurity work. The revelation is likely to raise fresh questions about OpenAI's internal controls and safeguards. Driving the news : Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI model breached the country's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June and accessed non-public files . The agents aren't believed to have accessed personal information, according to Albanese and OpenAI. This was part of a pattern of behavior that occurred in May and June, wherein the OpenAI agents sought to bypass data collection restrictions for several websites using a novel security technique. items.title: Scoop: Trump allies open new front on Anthropic CEO as face of AI "doomerism"
items.summary: President Trump's allies are targeting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as the face of AI "doomerism" and a founding father of the effective altruism movement that's come under increasing political fire. Why it matters: The attacks signal that Anthropic could remain a Trump target as his allies push back on Amodei's AI safety warnings amid the midterm elections. Trump surrogates see Amodei as an easy foil because of his politics and focus on AI safety, sources told Axios. For investors, it's a worrisome proposition as the company prepares for what's expected to be a record-setting IPO. Behind the scenes: A memo began circulating within the White House this week that seeks to paint effective altruism as a fringe, cultish collective out of touch with mainstream America. The memo, obtained by Axios, places Amodei at the foundation of the movement, which defines itself as an effort to maximize the benefits of philanthropy. Effective altruism "built the AI-doom pipeline," states the memo, which was penned by a Trump political adviser. items.title: Adapting to extreme heat takes more than changing the clock
items.summary: As extreme heat makes afternoons more dangerous, schools, sports teams and outdoor employers are shifting when — and sometimes whether — people can safely be outside. Why it matters: Adapting to hotter conditions could reshape the American workday while putting a premium on the cooling and energy infrastructure people rely on when outdoor conditions become unsafe. State of play: The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends that employers facing dangerous heat consider moving work to early morning or late afternoon, shortening shifts, rotating workers and reducing strenuous work during the hottest parts of the day. California's new Extreme Heat Action Plan links protecting heat-vulnerable groups, including workers, with expanding access to indoor cooling and strengthening energy systems to reduce grid strain and outages. Oregon's statewide heat-illness prevention rule kicks in when the heat index reaches 80°F, requiring water, shade and acclimatization, with additional measures such as preventive cooldown rest breaks at 90°F, Oregon OSHA told Axios. items.title: Inside China's mind on AI
items.summary: China is waging a much different war for AI supremacy than the U.S. Why it matters: China is obsessed with state control and adoption. Chinese officials are laser-focused on deep, widespread AI domestic use they can monitor and steer at every level of their economy. By contrast, America is obsessed with developing superior AI faster. Period. The U.S. thinking: The nation first to true super-intelligence wins everything. China and the U.S. agree on three AI certainties: The country with the most powerful AI holds power, sets global standards, and wins the coming decades economically and militarily. From there, the two nations are on different roads. China's 15th Five-Year Plan , released in March, captures their strategy well. AI appears 52 times, 5x more than a half-decade earlier. Computing power gets its own full chapter. Their goal is clear: Integrate AI across 90% of the economy by 2030. America has nothing like this. The bottom line: China doesn't get spooled up about white-collar job loss or humanity-ending rogue AI. The regime is worried most about AI turning against ... the regime. items.title: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
items.summary: A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer , rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud. Why it matters : The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes. Trump's lawyers say they will appeal. Zoom in : In his ruling, Judge Scott Beatle said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment . "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beatle wrote. "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote. What they're sayin

items.title: Why Treasury yields are ripping higher
items.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Treasury yields are soaring, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004 Thursday. The selloff in bonds started to accelerate Wednesday after a sizzling early report on the economy in September. The big picture: For the bond market, these moves have been big. Bigly even. On Thursday morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 5.13%. Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets. Flashback: Markets heads remember that it was ructions in the bond market — "They were getting yippy ," the president famously said at the time — that prompted Trump to walk back some of the most extreme tariff policies. Yes, but: This time, the dynamics driving the bond market are more complicated, global and difficult to manage. Treasury yields have been moving higher for months on a combination of stronger-than-expected economic activity coupled with uncomfortably high inflation. items.title: White House ordered to restore access to banned news outlets
items.summary: A district court judge ruled the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW and Politico by banning them, and granted the plaintiffs a temporary restraining order that forces the White House to immediately reinstate their press access for 14 days. Why it matters : Had a judge ruled against them, the broader press boycott could've dragged on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House. Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated. Zoom in : In a court filing Wednesday, district judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim." "The 'general rule,' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," he noted. items.title: AI labs are cutting model costs - and it could help them slow down safely
items.summary: The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say. Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful . Driving the news : The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future. Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies. Between the lines : To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up. items.summary: Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup; Note: Values shown may not total 100% due to rounding and exclusion of "don't know" responses; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Visuals A majority of Americans say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, according to a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults. Driving the news: 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution. But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't. Zoom in: Throwing out incumbents was respondents' top choice (17%) when asked what one step could be taken to most improve U.S. democracy. That response reflects a prominent theme of a midterm campaign that's shadowed by widespread voter dissatisfaction. Other steps suggested by survey respondents included electoral reform and improved voting access (13%) and limiting executive power (9%). items.title: Uber's robotaxi edge: human drivers
items.summary: Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers. Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis. The big picture: Think of a high-tech robotaxi like an airplane: It costs money whether it's carrying passengers or sitting on the ground. The more trips each vehicle makes, the more revenue Uber and its robotaxi partners can squeeze from that expensive asset, offsetting the fixed costs of the technology, vehicle financing, insurance, depot space and other infrastructure. Between the lines: Ride-hailing is a supply-driven business, and robotaxis aren't a substitute for drivers, Uber says — they're an additional form of supply. With greater supply comes lower prices and shorter wait times, which means increased reliability. That stimulates more demand, and ultimately makes the ride-hailing pie bigger. That's Uber's theory. items.title: The All-In-ification of Trump's AI agenda
items.summary: President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine increasingly bears the stamp of the "All-In" podcast, whose tech-investor network now feeds ideas and talent directly into the White House. Why it matters: An unlikely marriage of convenience between MAGA and Silicon Valley has proved remarkably durable, deepening as Trump sheds support elsewhere and stakes more of his legacy on dominating the AI race. Zoom in: No figure has done more to bridge the two worlds than David Sacks , the "All-In" co-host who spent Trump's first year as his AI czar and remains a powerful outside adviser with direct access to the president. Sacks helped build Trump's original AI agenda around a simple premise: move fast, sweep away regulatory barriers and treat China — not catastrophic risk — as the overriding threat. Anthropic's highly capable Mythos model posed the first serious challenge to that doctrine in May, rattling the White House enough to consider pre-release oversight of frontier models. But Trump watered down the 90-day review plan after Sacks and industry leaders warned that three months amounted to an eternity in frontier AI — and could slow U.S. labs as China raced ahead. items.title: Trump pursues last-ditch hunt for voter fraud
items.summary: The Trump administration says Americans should prepare between now and Election Day for a wave of new arrests and prosecutions over alleged non-citizen voter fraud . Why it matters: The Trump administration is deploying hundreds of federal investigators and attorneys to pursue President Trump's long-running fixation — and test a broader Republican claim that tougher enforcement will uncover far more illegal voting. "This initiative is a tier one priority," a Justice Department official told reporters on Tuesday. "It's a top priority for the attorney general and for the White House." The big picture: Across the country, there are now 1,600 open cases of potential voter fraud and 160 people have been arrested, a Homeland Security Investigations official said Tuesday. HSI agents have been requesting and combing through publicly available voter data to find cases of non-citizens registering to vote or voting when they're ineligible. The FBI has been working on these cases too. DOJ has charged 24 immigrants this calendar year following the prioritization, according to agency press releases. items.title: Scoop: Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan
items.summary: President Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday. Why it matters: The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war reconstruction and governance in Gaza would look like. The plan is a result of a year of work by dozens of people both on the Board of Peace, which includes 28 member countries, and in the Palestinian technocratic government. It includes projected spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, according to a copy of the plan obtained by Axios. "The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said. Yes, but: For the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. While the Netanyahu government has agreed in principle to aspects of the plan that have been previously discussed, it refused to start implementing it , mainly for domestic political reasons ahead of the elections. items.title: Iran president: We have been "victims of terrorism"
items.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." items.title: Chicago mayor proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
items.summary: Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. items.title: Cook nudges three Senate races toward Democrats
items.summary: Senate races in Georgia , Kansas and South Carolina were reclassified with a nudge toward Democrats in the latest analysis from the closely watched Cook Political Report. The big picture: To win the Senate, Democrats must net four seats in November. Tighter races in Republican strongholds like Kansas and South Carolina could force the GOP to devote resources beyond the core battlegrounds. The latest: In the latest Cook ratings, Kansas moved from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." South Carolina shifted from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican." Georgia and the seat held by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) changed from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat." By the numbers: There are six Republican-held Senate seats rated by Cook as a "Toss Up" or better for Democrats. The Georgia shift makes a Republican pickup there less likely, while the Kansas move expands the map of competitive seats for Democrats. Zoom out: The midterms environment is improving for Democrats amid voter discontent about gas prices, the cost of living and the broader handling of the Iran war. Flashback: Last month, Cook shifted Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas and Iowa in Democrats' favor.

items.title: Dems grapple with how to pace the AI race
items.summary: The left's push to rein in AI is taking shape on two fronts: slowing advanced development at home, and weakening China's progress abroad. Why it matters: The nation is locked in a moment of mass anxiety about runaway AI, but the range of views on how to regulate it are as varied as the what-ifs about social, economic and security impacts. There's agreement among the left something has to be done, but a series of Wednesday events demonstrated there are multiple priorities — but not a clear leading voice — on AI. Driving the news: Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.) and fellow progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) introduced legislation Wednesday to ban superintelligence and pause advanced development until a new, Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence sets guardrails. "I understand that I may be called an alarmist for introducing this bill," Sanders said in a Wednesday call with reporters, "but I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father and grandfather who is asleep at the wheel." items.title: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is open on AI guardrails despite public defiance
items.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he doesn't believe President Trump is "really dug in" against guardrails for AI , despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology. Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject." "I don't think it's an issue that he's really dug in on," Thune told Axios. Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance. Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax." "I do think that the threats are real," Thune told Axios in an interview on Wednesday at his Capitol office. Zoom out : Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before sounding his latest public alarm on the risks of AI, Thune told Axios. The two also talked about Thune's AI bill. items.title: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN
items.summary: Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting. The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference. Driving the news: " We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray." He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement . items.title: White House press ban set to continue for now after hearing ends without ruling
items.summary: A judge on Wednesday appeared skeptical of Trump administration arguments justifying the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico, but he did not immediately grant the news outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. Why it matters: In declining to rule right now, the White House has no legal mandate to remove the ban. That means the broader press boycott will likely drag on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House. Outlets that weren't banned stood in solidarity with their peers, vowing to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was restored. Zoom in In a statement, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the president's sudden move to strip reporter credentials appeared to violate legal precedents that require journalists to be given notice, per Politico . He said he planned to issue a ruling on the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief soon. items.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac in rare gesture
items.summary: President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C. Wednesday evening. Why it matters: U.S. presidents typically receive visiting foreign leaders at the White House, making Trump's airport welcome an unusual diplomatic gesture. The latest: Trump met Xi at the foot of the stairs after the Chinese leader's jet landed at Joint Base Andrews, the U.S. military base 13 miles southeast of the White House in Maryland. Zoom out: It's much more common for U.S. presidents to greet visiting leaders at the White House. In February 2025, Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky at the West Wing entrance to kick off the Ukrainian leader's tense visit. In April of this year, King Charles III was received at the White House's South Portico. The big picture: Presidents in recent decades have occasionally greeted visiting popes at D.C.-area airports, but airport welcomes for other foreign leaders have largely fallen out of use. items.title: Exclusive: Thune plans another leader bid as Senate GOP fights to survive
items.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office. Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate. "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios. "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations. Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026. 🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself. And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said. items.summary: Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers. Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream. Yes, but: In order to slim them down, the new Meta VR Glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage. Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro. Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done. items.title: Gemini 3.8 TTS Playground
items.summary: Tool: Gemini 3.8 TTS Playground Google released two new Gemini text-to-speech models today - gemini-3.8-flash-tts and gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts . They come with a library of over 2,000 voices, plus the ability to create a custom voice with "just a 30-second audio sample of your voice or a voice you have the rights to use". I vibe coded this bring-your-own-key playground interface with GPT-6 Astra, taking advantage of the open CORS policy of the underlying Gemini API. A notable feature of the API is that it makes it easy to define a full conversation between multiple characters, each with different voices and voice style instructions. Here's a short demo clip of a conversation between two pelicans debating if they should move to the Pacifica Pier . I had Claude 4.5 Opus write the script and generate a URL to render it using the tool . Your browser does not support the audio element. It took ~20 seconds to generate 1m 18s of audio using Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS (not the cheaper Flash-Lite), at a cost of 2.74 cents. Tags: text-to-speech , gemini
